# The Flesh

> "For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire."
>
> — Galatians 5:17

Let's get one thing straight before anything else. There is nothing wrong with your sex drive.

God made it, and he made it strong on purpose. In C.S. Lewis's *Screwtape Letters* a senior devil complains about exactly this: "He made the pleasures: all our research so far has not enabled us to produce one." The other side can't make a pleasure. It can only bend one. Desire for a woman is the reason any of us are here. It's meant to pull a man out of himself and towards a wife, a home and children. Nothing in this book is against desire, and nothing in it is against your body. One man who was bound by this habit for years, and now teaches other men about it, puts the whole matter in a line. The trouble, he says, is "the wrong use of the right thing. Pleasure is not bad."

When Paul writes about "the flesh", he doesn't mean your skin. He means the part of a man that wants what it wants, now, for itself, and doesn't care what it costs. If you're not a believer, call it appetite. Whatever you call it, you've met it.

Lust is what happens when the flesh gets hold of desire. Desire says, "She is lovely." Lust says, "I want that, for me, now." Desire looks at a person. Lust looks at something to use.

Lust has three faces, and you met them in the Introduction. The first is the screen: porn, and its quieter cousins in your feed. The second is the hand. The third is the chase: the messages, the flirting, the woman you know is wrong for you and can't leave alone. They look like three problems. They are one appetite going out through three doors.

Masturbation is the plainest case, so we'll use it to show how the thing works. A drive that was built to end in another person is made to end in a tissue. It's a hijacking, and the plane lands nowhere.

## How the loop works {-}

You'll find plenty of videos that explain this habit with brain chemistry, complete with diagrams. We're going to skip all of that. Some of it is shaky, and you don't need any of it. You don't have to understand an engine to notice that the car keeps pulling left.

What happens is simple, and you can check every step against your own experience.

1. **A cue.** You get into bed. You step into the shower. The house goes quiet. You're bored, or wound up, or lonely, or you saw something on your phone.
2. **An urge.** A small, restless "go on".
3. **Relief.** You do it, or you open the site, or you send the message. The restlessness stops.

That's the loop: cue, urge, relief. Every time you go round it, you teach yourself that this cue leads to that relief. Do it a few hundred times and the lesson is learned by heart. The cue alone will now produce the urge. It doesn't matter whether you're aroused, in the mood, or even paying attention.

It's like a shortcut across a lawn. The first time, you barely leave a mark. Walk the same line every night for ten years and there's a bare strip of earth, and your feet take it without asking you.

That's the whole mechanism. It needs no chemistry lesson. It doesn't mean you have a broken brain, an unusually high drive or a weak character. You have a path worn in the grass.

Notice one more thing. The urge isn't really desire for a woman. It's the wish to end a restless feeling. Hold on to that, because the rest of the chapter hangs on it.

## The Little Monster {-}

We'll call that restless urge the Little Monster.

The first thing to know about him is how small he is. Lewis had his measure: "Lust is a poor, weak, whimpering, whispering thing". The urge involves no pain at all. It's a faint, empty, fidgety sense that something is missing. That's why men mistake it for sex drive, or for hunger, or for plain boredom. Left alone for a while it can turn into edginess and a short temper. It's a hunger, but a hunger for something that doesn't feed you.

He's so small that most men have lived with him for decades without noticing he was there.

The name isn't ours alone, by the way. A twenty-year-old youth leader, a model Christian to everyone who knew him, wrote down his secret years before this book existed: "However, I had a little monster, on the inside, that kept gnawing at me slowly". He had never read a page of this method. He had simply met the same tenant.

In the first months you don't notice him at all. The itch and its relief are so slight that you'd laugh at the idea you were hooked. Later, when you're doing it most days, you tell yourself you've come to enjoy it, or that you've "got into the habit". By then the truth is that you already have a tenant. The Little Monster has moved in, and every so often you go round the loop to feed him.

One man in the trap put the entire thing in seven words:

> "I hate it, but I continually feed it."
>
> — a commenter on a Christian recovery blog

You met him in the introduction. He's worth hearing twice, because he has seen what most men never see. He doesn't say "I love it" or "I need it". He says he feeds it.

That is the only reason any man carries on, whether he does it three times a day or twice a month. He's feeding the Little Monster.

And the Little Monster isn't fussy. A video feeds him. A fantasy feeds him. A long look at a stranger feeds him, and so does a flirty message from a woman you have no business messaging. It's all one diet.

Here is the cruellest part. The "pleasure" a man gets from it is mostly the pleasure of getting back to how he'd have felt anyway. He's trying to return to the peace and ease he had as a boy, before any of this started. And he keeps using the very thing that took it from him.

## The annoying alarm {-}

Have you ever had a car alarm going in the street for half the afternoon? You stop hearing it after a while, but your shoulders don't. Then somebody finally shuts it off, and the quiet is wonderful.

But nothing wonderful has arrived. An irritation has ended.

That's what the relief is. Before the habit, you were complete. You had no alarm. Each time you go round the loop you feel better for a moment, and you also set the alarm to go off again. It isn't a pain. It's more like a tap dripping somewhere in the house.

Your reason doesn't follow any of this, and it doesn't need to. All you know is that there's an itch, you do the thing, and the itch goes. But it doesn't stay gone. The relief you just bought is what sets up the next urge. Men on the recovery forums have a name for this, the "chaser", and one of them described it with more honesty than dignity:

> "The chaser effect. It is real. After sex I could feel my crotch begging me to fap."
>
> — a man on a porn-recovery site

One coach on YouTube says the same in his own way: "the more you touch yourself the more thirsty you are".

And the man who called it the wrong use of the right thing saw what each round of relief was really building: "you think that you're relieving yourself by engaging in the sin, but you're making the stronghold more reinforced." He called it adding the brick and mortar to your own prison.

It's the oldest trick there is. It's like wearing shoes a size too small all day for the pleasure of kicking them off at night.

Why can't men see it like that? There are three reasons.

1. **You've been told since boyhood that it's natural and harmless.** There's a grain of truth in that, which is what makes it stick. We'll deal with it in the next chapter.
2. **The itch doesn't hurt.** It feels exactly like ordinary restlessness, tiredness or stress, and those are the very moments you reach for it. So you think of the feeling as normal life, and never as something the habit put there.
3. **It works back to front.** This is the big one. You suffer the empty feeling when you're *not* doing it, so you never blame the last time. And the moment you start, the feeling eases, so the habit gets the credit. The thing that causes the itch gets thanked for scratching it.

Think of a rash. Scratching it feels like bliss, and for a few seconds nothing on earth is better. It's also the reason the rash is still there next week. A man with clear skin doesn't lie awake wishing he had something to scratch.

Men say masturbation is "satisfying". But nobody can be satisfied who wasn't dissatisfied to begin with. The free man lies down at night and goes to sleep. He isn't satisfied, because he was never unsatisfied. You can't rest until the Little Monster has been fed.

## A pleasure or a crutch? {-}

Let me repeat the main point, because everything turns on it. Men find it hard to stop because they believe they'd be giving up a real pleasure or a real support. You need to see that you're giving up nothing at all.

The best way to see it is to compare the habit with eating, because it has disguised itself as eating.

Eat at regular times and you hardly notice hunger. Push a meal back and you feel it: no pain, just an empty, slightly edgy feeling. Then you eat, and satisfying that hunger is one of life's real pleasures.

The habit looks just the same. There's an empty feeling, you act, and you get relief. That resemblance is what fools us. "It's an appetite, like any other. A man has to eat."

In fact the two are opposites.

- **Food feeds you. This drains you.** You get up from a meal with more than you sat down with. You get up from this with less. The same coach is blunt about it: "there's no positives for touching yourself".
- **Food is good, and stays good.** You'll enjoy a roast dinner at eighty. Whatever this once was, it stopped being a treat years ago. It's a chore you do with one eye on the door.
- **Eating doesn't create hunger. It ends it.** The habit creates its own itch. Far from ending it, each time guarantees the next.

Is eating a habit? Try giving it up and see. It's a need, like breathing. People do have habits about when they eat and what, but eating itself isn't one. And although this book says "the habit" because it's convenient, masturbation isn't just a habit either. A man doesn't do it at eleven at night because eleven is when he does it. He does it to quiet the empty feeling that the last time left behind.

"But isn't sex a God-given appetite too?" It is. And that is the point. Sex with your wife is the meal. This is licking the photograph on the menu. It was never what the hunger was for. Sex is the one appetite a man was given in order to give it away. The habit turns it into something he keeps entirely for himself. A husband who'd carried the habit into his marriage came to see it plainly:

> "I've come to realize that masturbation, any way you slice it, is a selfish act"
>
> — a married man on a Christian recovery blog

Notice, too, where the excitement actually is. It's in the lead-up: the door clicking shut, the scroll, the search for the right video, the building of the scene. The end itself lasts seconds, and the flatness lands straight after. That's why so many men drag it out. The thrill was always in the chase.

## Crossing the red line {-}

Whatever you repeat goes stale. The memory that worked last month doesn't work this month. The video that shocked you last year bores you now. The Little Monster wants a bit more, or something new.

Porn is built on this. It never runs out of new, so a man can chase "a bit more" for hours, tab after tab, and finish emptier than he started. C.S. Lewis has his senior devil state the recipe: "An ever increasing craving for an ever diminishing pleasure is the formula."

The Puritan John Owen described this in 1656, long before anyone had a phone. Lust, he wrote, "is modest, as it were, in its first motions and proposals, but having once got footing in the heart by them, it constantly makes good its ground, and presseth on to some farther degrees in the same kind." It asks for very little at first, and it never stays there.

So the fantasy creeps. First it's nothing much. Then a memory. Then a woman you actually know: someone at work, a friend's wife, the girl two rows in front at church. Then a little help from the phone: a photo, a feed, a "harmless" video. Then porn, and then harder porn. One man traced his own route:

> "From there it would lead to erotic fiction, to amateur images, and then straight back to the hardcore porn videos"
>
> — a man writing in a recovery newsletter

Every man has a red line. "I only use my imagination." "I'd never think about a real person." "I'd never watch that kind of thing." "I'd never message her." And every man knows the tug of war that goes on at that line. His conscience pulls one way and the Little Monster the other. This is exactly what Paul is describing in the verse that opens this chapter. The flesh and the Spirit want opposite things, and you're the rope.

So you cross the line, or you go right up to it, and afterwards you feel better than you did ten minutes earlier. But you're more restless and less at peace than the man who never started. It's worse than the tight shoes, in fact, because with every year a bit more of the ache stays behind after the shoes come off.

Since the Little Monster wants feeding, you choose the times. They turn out to be two pairs of opposites:

- **Boredom and concentration.**
- **Stress and relaxation.**

What kind of medicine wakes you up and puts you to sleep, calms you down and gives you a lift? There's no such medicine. The habit does none of those things. It ends an itch that it created, and then you carry on with whatever you were doing. We'll go through the occasions one by one in a later chapter.

Are you thinking of retreating to a "milder" version? Imagination only, weekends only, never with a screen? Everything in this book applies to all of it. It's the same loop and the same monster.

And don't believe that only weak men get caught. It takes a fairly strong man to carry a secret like this for twenty years. He has held down a job, a marriage and a place on the church rota the whole time.

## The dance around the red line {-}

Some men take a certain pride in their line. "I'm not like those guys. I never look at anything. It's all in my head."

Ask that man a question. "Suppose your usual wasn't available tonight. The favourite memory has worn out and the imagination won't start. Do you roll over and go to sleep?"

NOT A CHANCE.

A man will jerk off to anything. A stranger's holiday photos. An advert for swimwear. A scene from a film he'd be embarrassed to admit he watched. One coach tells of a caller on one of his livestreams. The man had done it so much that he'd started on girls dancing on TikTok, just to feel something. His verdict on the state we get ourselves into: "you'll do anything to get some kind of release".

We do it when we're ill. We do it when we're exhausted, when we're sad and when we aren't remotely in the mood. Married men do it an hour after making love to their wives. Does that sound like enjoyment to you? It sounds like a man feeding something.

## Thinking with the wrong head {-}

The same monster makes decisions for you outside the bedroom.

You know the list, because you've lived some of it. You text an old girlfriend at midnight. You stay in something you know is wrong, because leaving means going without. You spend money you haven't got on a woman who barely likes you. You tell a lie to keep a door open. You can't say no to the pretty one at work, so you do her job as well as your own.

In every case you'd tell a friend he was being a fool. In every case the reasons you gave yourself were made up afterwards. The decision was already taken, lower down.

This is the same loop: cue, urge, relief. A woman pays you attention, the itch stirs, and you do whatever makes it stop. It isn't love and it isn't courage. A man who loves a woman can think. A man led by the itch can't, and anyone who spots it can lead him. He is the soldier from the first page, taking his orders from the bottle. Chapter 8 comes back to that.

## Good news, twice {-}

Some men find all this alarming. "So I'm hooked. That makes it worse." No. It's the best news you've had in years, for two reasons.

**First:** the reason we carry on is that we think there's something in it for us. We know the costs are bigger than the gains. But we believe in the gains, and we picture a gap in our lives if it went. There is no gap. The habit doesn't give you anything. It takes.

**Second:** you are not badly hooked. You never were. The Little Monster is a pipsqueak. The urge, by itself, is so faint that you've mistaken it for boredom for half your life.

Then why do so many men find stopping so hard, suffer for months, and still long for it years later? Because of the second cause, the lies, which are next. The flesh on its own is easy to handle, and you can prove that from your own life.

## The smoker on the plane {-}

Take a twenty-a-day smoker. Ask him to go ten hours without a cigarette at home and he'll be climbing the curtains by lunchtime. Put the same man on a long flight and he sits there for ten hours. He eats his little tray of chicken, watches two films and causes no trouble at all. He knows there's no chance, so the craving doesn't bother to show up.

You're the same. Think of the week you spent at your in-laws, sleeping in the spare room with the thin walls. Think of the camping trip with the men from church. Think of the conference where you shared a twin room with a colleague. Think of basic training, where a soldier hasn't a minute to himself for a month. Did you suffer? You hardly thought about it. You went days, and it cost you nothing.

Then you got home, shut the bedroom door, and the Little Monster was up and shouting before you'd unpacked.

So what changed? Your body didn't. It was the same body in the tent as in the bedroom. What changed was that the cue came back, and with it the expectation. The Little Monster keeps quiet when he knows nothing is coming, and he wakes up the second it might be. What you felt wasn't need. It was expectation.

That means the fleshly part of this is easy to live with, even now, while you're still in it. It's why some men do it once a fortnight all their lives and are every bit as caught as the man who does it daily. It's also why a man can go a year clean, have "just one", and find the path across the lawn still there waiting for him.

So the flesh is not the main problem. It's the hook that the real problem hangs on. Don't think the damage is exaggerated, though. Ask any man who's been at it for twenty years what it has taken from him. But you may have heard that the path is worn in for life, and that's false. Grass grows back. Once you stop walking the line, the Little Monster starves, and he starves fast.

It's never too late. One of the men you met in the introduction got free in his forty-third year. If you've been at this for decades, or several times a day, take heart. It's just as easy for you as for the occasional user, and in one way it's better. The further down it has taken you, the bigger the relief. Men go from daily to nothing in one step. The so-called withdrawal is a few restless evenings, and a man can even enjoy them, because he knows what is dying.

One last thing before we move on. Read the opening verse again. Paul never says the flesh is beaten by more flesh, by a harder jaw and a tighter fist. The sentence just before it reads: "But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won't fulfill the lust of the flesh." (Galatians 5:16). He names what you walk towards and says nothing about pushing against. A few verses later he lists what grows in a man who walks that way, and the last item on the list is self-control. He calls it a fruit, which is something that grows on a tree. Nobody ever got an apple by clenching his teeth.

A man who can't control his lust can't be trusted. But the control doesn't come from straining. It comes when the lies are gone and there's nothing left to strain against.

So first, we deal with the lies.
